title: Why your 1 TB drive only shows 931 GB
description:
Drive makers count like the metric system: a terabyte is a trillion bytes. Windows counts in powers of 2, so its 'kilobyte' is 1,024 bytes, 2.4% bigger, and the gap compounds at every prefix: 4.9% at mega, 7.4% at giga, almost 10% at tera. Divide a trillion bytes by 1,024 three times and you get 931, which Windows labels GB. Nothing is missing; macOS counts by 1,000 and shows the same drive as 1 TB. Western Digital settled a class action over exactly this in 2006 and added a disclaimer to its packaging.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py). Sources: Wikipedia, Binary prefix; Apple Support, How iOS and macOS report storage capacity.

social_caption: Your 1 TB drive shows 931 GB, and not one byte is missing. Here's the counting mix-up behind it.
facts_checked: Drive makers use decimal SI prefixes (1 TB = 10^12 bytes); Windows uses MB/GB for binary sizes, so a '300 GB' drive appears as 279.4 GB; Western Digital (Safier v. Western Digital) settled in March 2006 and agreed to add a disclaimer to packaging and advertising; IEC binary prefixes (kibi, gibi) published 1999; binary units 2.4% / 4.9% / 7.4% / 10.0% bigger (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_prefix)
Apple: iOS 10 and earlier and OS X Leopard and earlier report storage in binary; later versions in decimal, 1 TB = 1 trillion bytes (https://support.apple.com/en-us/102119)

beats.say: Your 1 terabyte drive shows just 931 gigabytes.
It's not broken, and it's not hidden system files. Every single byte is there.
The box and your computer both count bytes. They just disagree on what giga means.
The maker counts in thousands. A kilobyte is 1,000 bytes, so a terabyte is a trillion bytes.
Windows counts in twos. Its kilobyte is 1,024 bytes. That's 2.4% bigger.
2.4% is nothing. But it stacks up at every step.
A megabyte is 4.9% bigger. A gigabyte, 7.4%. A terabyte, almost 10.
So take your trillion bytes and divide by 1,024 three times. 931.
Same trillion bytes, just counted in bigger buckets. A Mac counts by thousands, and shows 1 terabyte.
Western Digital got sued over this, and settled in 2006 by adding the fine print to the box.
So your 500 gigabyte drive. How many does Windows show?
